title: The Basel Problem — A Light-Based Proof
hook: The video opens by posing a 90-year-unsolved sum and immediately revealing the shocking answer π²/6, then asking 'What is π doing here?' to earn curiosity.

scenes.purpose: Establish the mystery: a numerical series equals something involving π

on_screen.desc: Number line with colored cumulative-sum rectangles growing term by term
Running decimal approximation with ??? beneath it
Morty pi-creature looking confused

scenes.transition: Rectangles and number line persist; question marks replaced by π²/6 reveal
scenes.narration_gist: This sum remained unsolved for 90 years until Euler found the shocking answer π²/6 — but what is π doing here?

scenes.purpose: Motivate the geometric approach by linking π to circles and introducing light as the physical model

on_screen.desc: Basel sum with π²/6 answer shown
Web-of-mathematics dot graph with highlighted path leading to a circle
Small circle with rotating radius tracing π
Glowing ambient light centered on the π symbol

scenes.transition: Web fades; scene cuts to a number line with lighthouses
scenes.narration_gist: Whenever π appears there is a path back to circles, and for the Basel problem that path runs through light.

scenes.purpose: Physically encode the Basel series as lighthouses on a number line

on_screen.desc: Horizontal number line with lighthouse icons at integers 1–5+
Ambient light glow radiating from each lighthouse
Morty at origin receiving light
Thought-bubble light indicator showing cumulative brightness reading

scenes.transition: Lighthouses switch on one by one; indicator value climbs toward π²/6
scenes.narration_gist: Place a lighthouse at every positive integer — the inverse-square law makes the total brightness equal exactly the Basel sum.

scenes.purpose: Introduce the inverse-square law and solidify why each lighthouse contributes 1/n²

on_screen.desc: Single light source with expanding concentric shells and copy-screens at distances 1, 2, 3
Brightness ∝ 1/distance² annotation
3-D cone version showing solid-angle spreading
Labels: 1× screen, 4× screen, 9× screen at respective distances

scenes.transition: 3-D scene dissolves back to 2-D lake geometry
scenes.narration_gist: Because area grows as distance squared, brightness falls as 1/distance² — that's the inverse-square law, and it's why lighthouses give us 1/n².

scenes.purpose: Derive the Inverse Pythagorean Theorem as the key transformation tool

on_screen.desc: Right triangle with observer at C, lighthouse at H, new lighthouses at A and B on axes
1/a² + 1/b² = 1/h² labeled in matching colors
Mini-triangle hypotenuse acting as a screen receiving identical light rays
'Inverse Pythagorean Theorem' title with surrounding box

scenes.transition: Triangle kept; circle geometry introduced around it
scenes.narration_gist: One lighthouse at H can be split into two at A and B on perpendicular axes with the same total brightness — the Inverse Pythagorean Theorem.

scenes.purpose: Set up the circular lake construction and its initial brightness

on_screen.desc: Small circle (circumference 2) with observer at one end, single lighthouse directly opposite
Brightness = π²/4 derived from diameter = 2/π
Tangent line at top of small circle touching larger circle of circumference 4
Two new lighthouses A and B marked on larger circle

scenes.transition: Small circle remains as reference; larger circle grows around it
scenes.narration_gist: Standing opposite a lighthouse on a lake of circumference 2 gives brightness π²/4, and drawing a tangent splits that into two lighthouses on a double-sized circle.

scenes.purpose: Iterate the doubling process, showing lighthouses stay evenly spaced

on_screen.desc: Nested circles of circumference 2, 4, 8 with lighthouses migrating outward
Lines through circle centers marking right angles via inscribed-angle theorem
Arc-spacing labels: 1, 2, 2, 2, 1 then all-2 at each step
Total brightness = π²/4 annotation persists across steps

scenes.transition: Circles expand to infinite radius; circles flatten to a line
scenes.narration_gist: Each doubling replaces every lighthouse with two evenly spaced ones on a bigger circle, keeping total brightness π²/4 at every stage.

scenes.purpose: Reveal the limiting infinite number line of odd-integer lighthouses summing to π²/4

on_screen.desc: Flat horizontal number line with lighthouses at all odd integers …−5,−3,−1,1,3,5…
∑ 1/n² (odd n, both signs) = π²/4
Observer dot at origin
Connection label: 'infinite circle limit'

scenes.transition: Full line kept; algebra panel introduced to the right
scenes.narration_gist: In the limit the circles become a line, and summing brightness over all odd integers gives π²/4 — the number line is a limit of ever-growing circles.

scenes.purpose: Bridge from odd-integer sum to the full Basel sum via scaling algebra

on_screen.desc: Sum over positive odd integers = π²/8
Missing even-integer sum = (1/4) × total, shown as scaled copy of lighthouses
Odds = (3/4) × total  →  total = (4/3) × π²/8
Final answer: π²/6 highlighted in yellow

scenes.transition: All elements fade; credit card for Ben Hambrecht appears
scenes.narration_gist: Restricting to one side gives π²/8; the even terms are a quarter-scaled copy of the whole sum, so multiplying by 4/3 yields π²/6.

lessons: Open with the answer before the proof so the audience spends the video understanding why, not just waiting to learn what.
Anchor abstract series to a physical model (light, area, distance) so the audience has an intuition to grab before any formula appears.
Introduce one reusable transformation rule (here: splitting a lighthouse into two) and let the rest of the proof be repetitive application of that rule, so complexity grows without cognitive load.
Keep a running 'invariant' label (brightness = π²/4) on screen through every transformation step so viewers always know what is being preserved.
Use nested geometry (circles inside circles) as an on-screen animation rather than a static diagram, letting the limiting process be visually obvious before it is stated in words.
Save the algebraic clean-up (odd→all integers) for a distinct final scene so the geometric payoff lands cleanly before bookkeeping begins.
tags: pi basel sum squares infinite series lighthouse inverse geometry
